messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid People: avoid other people, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

When Arjun was nine years old, his father began locking him in the basement closet as punishment. The routine was always the same: a sharp word, a shove, the heavy door slamming shut, and then the click of the bolt. The closet was unfinished—bare concrete walls, a single bulb that stayed off because the pull chain was too high. In winter, the cold seeped through the floorboards and settled on his skin like a second layer. He would curl into himself, shivering, listening to the muffled sounds of the house above, waiting for hours until his mother let him out. The cold was the worst part. It clung to him, made his fingers stiff, his teeth chatter. And the silence. He learned to dread the moment the door closed, the thud of metal against frame, because it meant he was alone with the temperature and his own fear.

Those nights never fully left him. Now, at thirty-six, Arjun is a detective with the city police. He is good at his job—meticulous, patient, able to sit through hours of interrogation without breaking his composure. Colleagues respect him. His wife, Priya, describes him as steady. But he knows that is a mask. Inside, he feels like the boy in the closet: cold, trapped, certain that something about him is fundamentally wrong. His reactions since the abuse, he believes, prove that he is a lousy coper. What kind of person, he thinks, still flinches at a door slamming thirty years later? He has come to see himself as defective, and that belief has hollowed out his sense of who he is. He used to know himself—a determined officer, a good husband, someone who could handle pressure. Now he is not sure what remains.

The triggers surface in mundane moments. At the precinct, every time a door opens or shuts—especially if it is heavy or slammed—his stomach drops. He has learned to brace himself, but the startle response still flickers across his face. Worse is the temperature. In the winter, walking into a cold room makes his skin prickle with dread. He keeps his office warm, but the sensation can ambush him: a draft through a window, the chill of a metal chair. He has started avoiding other people to minimise the risk of being caught off guard. During shift change, he stays at his desk until the hallway is empty. He turns down dinner invitations from colleagues. Priya has noticed he no longer wants to go out on weekends—he makes excuses about fatigue, about a case that needs his attention. Outings mean unpredictable sounds, sudden breezes, crowds where he cannot control what touches him.

Sleeping alone is the hardest. He and Priya share a bed, but when she works late or travels, Arjun cannot bring himself to lie down. The silence, the empty space beside him, the faint cold of unoccupied sheets—it all pulls him back to the basement. So he stays up, often until two or three in the morning, watching television or scrolling through case files. He tells himself he is being productive, but really he is delaying the moment he must face the bed. When he finally does sleep, it is shallow and broken by dreams he cannot fully recall. The fatigue accumulates. He has missed two morning briefings in the past month, something that never happened before. His sergeant pulled him aside with a look of concern, but Arjun deflected. He cannot explain that the real problem is his own memory, that he feels like he is coming apart.

What finally brought him to seek help was a minor incident that became unbearable. Last week, during a traffic stop, a patrol car door slammed shut next to him. The sound was sharp and close, and Arjun froze. His hand went to his weapon before he could stop it. The officer beside him gave him a strange look. Arjun laughed it off, but that night he could not sleep at all. He sat on the couch, his skin cold despite the heating, and thought about the boy in the closet. He realised he had been trying to outrun that closet his whole life—by becoming a detective, by staying busy, by never showing weakness—but it had followed him here. He has started therapy because he is terrified of losing what is left: his marriage, his career, the thin thread of who he used to be. He hopes, though he barely dares admit it, that maybe he can learn to let the door close without feeling the cold.
